title: Position: Text Embeddings Should Capture Implicit Semantics, Not Just Surface Meaning
claim: Strong models gain large margins over a lexical baseline on surface tasks but only small gains on implicit-meaning tasks.
layout: 1 panel bar chart, two color-coded groups, shaded hatched gap with red arrows
description: A single bar chart with the y-axis labeled Average Performance Gain (%), running from 0 to about 33. The left group is titled Surface Meaning. It has three light green bars for Stella, GTE-Qwen and Jasper, each at about 31-33%. The right group is titled Implicit Semantics. It has three light orange bars for E5-Mistral, OpenAI-L and GTE-Qwen, each at about 13%. caption: Average gains over a lexical baseline (Bag-of-Tokens) for SOTA embedding models on Surface Meaning versus Implicit Semantics. Surface performance is averaged over MTEB classification tasks [ref], while implicit-semantics performance is averaged over seven datasets probing pragmatic, attitudinal, and social meaning (Table [ref]). The comparison illustrates a performance divide: modern embeddings show large gains on surface-semantic benchmarks but much smaller gains on tasks requiring implicit interpretation.
abstract: This position paper argues that text embedding research should move beyond surface meaning and embrace implicit semantics as a central modeling objective. Text embeddings are a foundational component of modern NLP, underpinning a wide range of applications and driving sustained research progress. Despite rapid progress, most embedding models remain narrowly focused on surface-level semantics, whereas linguistic theory emphasizes that much of human meaning is implicit, shaped by pragmatics, speaker intent, and sociocultural context. Current models are typically trained on datasets that lack such depth and evaluated using benchmarks that reward surface similarity. As a result, they struggle with tasks that require interpretive reasoning, stance recognition, or socially grounded understanding. Our pilot study makes this limitation explicit, showing that even state-of-the-art embeddings achieve only marginal improvements over simple lexical baselines on tasks probing implicit semantics. We therefore call for a paradigm shift: embedding research should prioritize linguistically grounded and diverse training data, develop benchmarks that probe deeper semantic understanding, and treat implicit meaning as a core modeling objective to better align embeddings with real-world language complexity. The code is available at http://github.com/dukesun99/Implicit-Embeddings.
